description: validation of an internationalized e-mail addresses

tests.description: all string formats ignore integers
all string formats ignore floats
all string formats ignore objects
all string formats ignore arrays
all string formats ignore booleans
all string formats ignore nulls
a valid idn e-mail (example@example.test in Hangul)
an invalid e-mail/idn e-mail address
a valid e-mail address
a non-ASCII local part with an ASCII domain is valid
a non-ASCII quoted local part is valid
a domain label that is not in Unicode NFC is valid
a local part that is not in Unicode NFC is valid
a C1 control in the local part is valid
a noncharacter in the local part is valid
a local part at the 64-octet limit is valid
tests.comment: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321#section-4.5.3.1 every implementation must be able to receive a local part of 64 octets

tests.description: a fullwidth commercial at is not a local-part separator
tests.comment: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321#section-4.1.2 Mailbox = Local-part "@" ( Domain / address-literal ) splits on U+0040, and any IDN mapping applies only to the domain that split produces, so U+FF20 cannot become the delimiter

tests.description: a local part with a supplementary-plane character is valid
tests.comment: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6531#section-3.3 atext =/ UTF8-non-ascii, and https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629#section-4 UTF8-4 covers U+10000 and above

tests.description: a non-ASCII local part with an IPv4-address-literal is valid
tests.comment: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321#section-4.1.3 address-literal = "[" IPv4-address-literal "]"; RFC 6531 does not change it

tests.description: a non-ASCII local part with an IPv6-address-literal is valid
an octet greater than 255 in an address-literal is invalid
tests.comment: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321#section-4.1.3 Snum is a decimal integer in the range 0 through 255

tests.description: leading zeros in an address-literal octet are valid
tests.comment: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321#section-4.1.3 Snum = 1*3DIGIT representing 0 through 255, which permits leading zeros unlike the dec-octet rule behind the ipv4 format
